bib.title: The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Chapter 18: High-Dimensional Problems: p >> N

question: How should prediction and feature assessment be done when the number of features p is much larger than the number of observations N?
hypothesis: When p >> N, high variance and overfitting dominate, so simple, heavily regularized methods (and FDR-style multiple-testing control for feature assessment) work best.
contributions: Prediction in p >> N: diagonal LDA and nearest shrunken centroids, quadratic-penalty linear classifiers (RDA, ridge logistic, SVM) with an SVD shortcut, L1 and elastic-net classifiers, the fused lasso, kernel and inner-product methods when features are unavailable, supervised principal components and pre-conditioning.
Feature assessment: permutation t-tests, Bonferroni/FWER, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, the plug-in FDR estimate, SAM, pFDR, q-value and local FDR.

limits: Test-set sizes are small (20, 34, 54, 108 samples; 48 abstracts); the authors state the test-error SE in Table 18.1 is about 3 and 4.5 in Table 18.2, so rankings among the top methods are inconclusive.
Supervised PC simulation (18.37) is described by the authors as seeming 'tailor-made' for the method; they point to Bair et al. (2006) for other data.
The authors have no explanation for why RFE hurts the SVM on the 14-class data (p.659).
The chapter is a 2009 text built around microarrays and early proteomics; no deep learning, no stability selection, and no modern post-selection inference.

FDR plug-in estimate is not corrected by M0/M, so it is conservative; the permutation null treats all genes as exchangeable and the independence assumption in the BH proof is acknowledged to fail for genes.
Lasso on mass spectra is not scientifically interpretable (weights not at peaks); the peak-extraction version trades accuracy (28 vs 22 errors) for interpretability.
practices: When p >> N, prefer simple, heavily regularized models; shrink all the way down when signal is spread over many weak coefficients (Sec 18.1, Fig 18.1).

Use diagonal LDA, then nearest shrunken centroids with soft thresholding of standardized class-mean differences, with Delta by 10-fold CV, to get a classifier with built-in feature selection (Sec 18.2).
Standardize each patient/profile when the shape of the profile matters more than absolute level (Sec 18.3, 14-class example).

Quadratic-penalty linear models (ridge, RDA, logistic, SVM) can be fit in the N-dimensional row space using the SVD, and R can be computed once for all CV folds (Sec 18.3.5, Ex 18.12); the trick does not apply to the lasso.
Use L1 or elastic-net penalties when feature selection is needed; use the elastic net when correlated features should be averaged and more than N nonzero coefficients are wanted (Sec 18.4).
Use the fused lasso when features are ordered along an index, to get sparse and piecewise-constant coefficients (Sec 18.4.2).

If only a similarity matrix is available, kernelize: SVM, nearest centroid, 1-NN and PCA all work from inner products or double-centered distances, but standardization and per-feature assessment are lost (Secs 18.5.1-18.5.2).

For censored-survival or regression with many noisy features, screen features by univariate association, take leading PCs of the survivors, and choose threshold and number of PCs by CV (Algorithm 18.1).
To get sparsity with supervised PC accuracy, fit the lasso to the supervised-PC prediction (pre-conditioning) (Sec 18.6.3).
For feature assessment use permutation-based p-values, preferably pooled across genes, and control FDR rather than FWER when M is large (Sec 18.7).
FDR bounds as large as 0.15 can be acceptable for exploratory microarray work since FDR is not type-I error (p.690).
Use SAM with asymmetric cutpoints when differentially expressed genes move mostly in one direction (Sec 18.7.2).

terms.definition: prediction problems in which the number of features p is much larger than the number of observations N
LDA with a diagonal within-class covariance; equivalent to nearest centroid after standardization and a special case of naive Bayes
diagonal LDA with class means shrunk toward the overall mean by soft thresholding d'_kj = sign(d_kj)(|d_kj| - Delta)+
sign(x)(|x| - Delta)+; each value reduced by Delta in absolute value and set to zero if it would cross zero
backward stepwise removal of genes with the smallest coefficients, refitting the classifier
sum_j (alpha|beta_j| + (1-alpha) beta_j^2); a compromise between lasso and ridge that averages correlated features
lasso with an extra penalty lambda2 sum |beta_{j+1} - beta_j| encouraging smoothness in the feature index
inner product of counts of all length-m subsequences of two strings, K_m(x1,x2) = <Phi_m(x1), Phi_m(x2)>
the observation with the smallest average distance to the other observations in its class
screen features by univariate association with the outcome, then regress on the leading principal components of the retained features
select features as in supervised PC, then apply partial least squares to them
fit the lasso to a denoised outcome (supervised-PC prediction) using all features
the probability of at least one false rejection, Pr(V >= 1)
reject H0j if p_j < alpha/M, giving FWER <= alpha
FDR = E(V/R), the expected proportion of falsely rejected nulls among the R rejections
L = max{j : p(j) < alpha*j/M}; reject all hypotheses with p_j <= p(L)
estimated FDR = E_hat(V)/R_obs, where E_hat(V) is the mean number of permutation statistics beyond the cut-point
reject when |t(j) - expected permutation order statistic t~(j)| > Delta, allowing asymmetric cutpoints
E(V/R | R > 0), equal to Pr(Z_j = 0 | t_j in Gamma) under the mixture model
the smallest FDR over all rejection regions that reject t_j
Pr(Z_j = 0 | t_j = t0), the FDR for an infinitesimal rejection region around t0
